title: Energy system modelling for the energy transition
about: Curated high-quality literature: assessment reports, meta-studies, systematic reviews, model intercomparisons, methodological standards and landmark modelling studies. Key findings are short paraphrases; read the originals before citing.

categories.label: Assessments & scenario databases
categories.blurb: Consensus reports and large scenario ensembles. Start here.

categories.label: Meta-studies & model intercomparisons
categories.blurb: Studies that synthesise many studies or run many models on the same question.

categories.label: Reviews of models & tools
categories.blurb: Systematic and narrative reviews of the modelling landscape.

categories.label: Methods & good practice
categories.blurb: How to model well: uncertainty, resolution, alternatives, openness.

categories.label: Track record & assumptions
categories.blurb: Ex-post checks of how past projections performed and why.

categories.label: Landmark modelling studies
categories.blurb: Single studies that shaped the debate, from top journals.

items.title: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change — Chapter 6: Energy Systems
items.authors: Clarke, L., Wei, Y.-M., et al.
items.venue: IPCC AR6 Working Group III, Cambridge University Press
items.finding: Limiting warming to 1.5–2 °C requires energy-sector CO2 to reach net zero around mid-century, through electrification, efficiency, a rapid build-out of low-carbon supply and a phase-down of unabated fossil fuels. The roles of nuclear and CCS vary widely across pathways.
items.why: The broadest consensus assessment available, synthesising thousands of peer-reviewed studies.

items.title: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change — Chapter 3: Mitigation pathways compatible with long-term goals
items.authors: Riahi, K., Schaeffer, R., et al.
items.venue: IPCC AR6 Working Group III, Cambridge University Press
items.finding: Assesses the full AR6 ensemble of integrated-assessment pathways by warming category, showing which system changes are robust across models and which depend on model choice.
items.why: The definitive meta-analysis of global integrated assessment model (IAM) scenarios.

items.title: AR6 Scenarios Database
items.authors: Byers, E., Krey, V., Kriegler, E., Riahi, K., et al.
items.finding: Open, harmonised dataset of the model pathways behind AR6. You can pull your own ranges, e.g. nuclear, wind or solar shares by warming category.
items.why: Lets you check claims about 'what the models say' directly against the data.

items.title: Net Zero Roadmap: A Global Pathway to Keep the 1.5 °C Goal in Reach (2023 update)
items.authors: International Energy Agency
items.finding: Normative 1.5 °C pathway built on tripling renewable capacity and doubling efficiency gains by 2030, with nuclear capacity also expanding substantially by 2050.
items.why: Highly influential and detailed, but a single-model pathway — compare it with the IPCC ranges.

items.title: The Costs of Decarbonisation: System Costs with High Shares of Nuclear and Renewables
items.authors: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency
items.finding: Plant-level costs understate the full cost of high variable-renewable systems; grid, balancing and profile costs rise with the VRE share. In the cases modelled, mixes keeping dispatchable low-carbon capacity had lower total system cost.
items.why: Clear, widely cited framework for system costs. Read with the publisher's nuclear mandate in mind.

items.title: The Future of Nuclear Energy in a Carbon-Constrained World
items.authors: MIT Energy Initiative
items.finding: Excluding nuclear raises the cost of deep power-sector decarbonisation in the regions modelled; construction cost is the central barrier, and the study focuses on how to cut it.
items.why: Major interdisciplinary study pairing system modelling with cost analysis of nuclear construction.

items.title: Energieperspektiven 2050+ (Swiss Energy Perspectives 2050+)
items.authors: Prognos, TEP Energy, Infras, Ecoplan for the Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE/BFE)
items.finding: The Swiss government's reference scenarios for reaching net zero by 2050, covering demand, supply and the electricity system.
items.why: The official modelling basis for Swiss energy and climate policy.

items.title: Getting to Zero Carbon Emissions in the Electric Power Sector
items.authors: Jenkins, J.D., Luke, M., Thernstrom, S.
items.finding: Across roughly 40 decarbonisation studies, cutting power-sector CO2 by half to two-thirds is relatively easy; getting to near zero is much harder and cheapest with a diverse portfolio that includes firm low-carbon resources (nuclear, CCS, geothermal, etc.).
items.why: The most cited synthesis on the 'last 10–20%' problem in power decarbonisation.

items.title: Burden of proof: A comprehensive review of the feasibility of 100% renewable-electricity systems
items.authors: Heard, B.P., Brook, B.W., Wigley, T.M.L., Bradshaw, C.J.A.
items.finding: Scored 24 100%-renewable studies against feasibility criteria (demand, time resolution, transmission, reliability) and concluded none fully met them.
items.why: Sharpest critique of the 100%-RE literature. Read together with the Brown et al. (2018) response.

items.title: Response to 'Burden of proof: A comprehensive review of the feasibility of 100% renewable-electricity systems'
items.authors: Brown, T.W., Bischof-Niemz, T., Blok, K., Breyer, C., Lund, H., Mathiesen, B.V.
items.finding: Rebuts the feasibility criteria point by point and argues the technical issues raised are addressed in the literature, so 100% RE systems are feasible and economically viable.
items.why: The main counter-argument; together with Heard et al. it maps the core of the debate.

items.title: Status and perspectives on 100% renewable energy systems
items.authors: Hansen, K., Breyer, C., Lund, H.
items.finding: Reviews the fast-growing body of 100% RE studies: feasibility and comparable costs are a common conclusion, with a shift towards cross-sector, sector-coupled models.
items.why: Good map of the 100% RE research field and its main groups.

items.title: On the History and Future of 100% Renewable Energy Systems Research
items.authors: Breyer, C., Khalili, S., Bogdanov, D., et al.
items.finding: Traces 100% RE research from its origins; argues feasibility is now well established and the frontier is pace, sector coupling and global coverage.
items.why: Most comprehensive history of the field, written by its core community.

items.title: Emissions and energy impacts of the Inflation Reduction Act
items.authors: Bistline, J., Blanford, G., Brown, M., et al.
items.finding: Nine models project US economy-wide emissions 43–48% below 2005 by 2035 with the IRA, versus 27–35% without it.
items.why: Textbook example of a multi-model study separating robust from model-specific results.

items.title: Power sector impacts of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022
items.authors: Bistline, J.E.T., Brown, M., Domeshek, M., et al.
items.finding: Across 11 models, US power-sector CO2 falls 66–87% below 2005 by 2035 with the IRA; the low-emitting share (renewables, nuclear, CCS) reaches 59–89%.
items.why: Power-sector deep dive with an unusually large model ensemble.

items.title: Modeling nuclear energy's future role in decarbonized energy systems
items.authors: Bistline, J., Bragg-Sitton, S., Cole, W., et al.
items.finding: Nuclear deployment in models is highest when stringent climate policy, nuclear cost reductions and limits on competing technologies coincide, so results hinge on those assumptions.
items.why: Key read for interpreting any model's nuclear result; written by EPRI, NREL, INL and other labs.

items.title: Looking under the hood: A comparison of techno-economic assumptions across national and global integrated assessment models
items.authors: Krey, V., Guo, F., Kolp, P., et al.
items.finding: Cost and performance assumptions differ widely between IAMs and are often poorly documented, which explains much of the divergence in their results.
items.why: Shows why you should always check the input assumptions behind a scenario.

items.title: Energy systems modeling for twenty-first century energy challenges
items.authors: Pfenninger, S., Hawkes, A., Keirstead, J.
items.finding: Classifies model families (optimisation, simulation, power-system/market, qualitative) and names the core challenges: time and space resolution, uncertainty and transparency, complexity, and human behaviour.
items.why: The standard entry point to the field; still widely cited.

items.title: A review of modelling tools for energy and electricity systems with large shares of variable renewables
items.authors: Ringkjøb, H.-K., Haugan, P.M., Solbrekke, I.M.
items.finding: Compares 75 tools on how well they capture variable renewables; short-term variability and flexibility are often underrepresented in long-term models.
items.why: Best reference for choosing a tool for high-renewable systems.

items.title: A review of current challenges and trends in energy systems modeling
items.authors: Lopion, P., Markewitz, P., Robinius, M., Stolten, D.
items.finding: Trends toward higher temporal and spatial resolution, sector coupling and open source, in tension with computational tractability.
items.why: Concise snapshot of where the field was heading.

items.title: Classification and challenges of bottom-up energy system models — A review
items.authors: Prina, M.G., Manzolini, G., Moser, D., Nastasi, B., Sparber, W.
items.finding: Classifies bottom-up models by resolution (time, space, techno-economic detail, sector coupling) and maps the trade-offs between them.
items.why: Clear classification scheme useful for reading model descriptions.

items.title: Trends in tools and approaches for modelling the energy transition
items.authors: Chang, M., Thellufsen, J.Z., Zakeri, B., Pickering, B., Pfenninger, S., Lund, H., Østergaard, P.A.
items.finding: Reviews earlier reviews and surveys 54 tools directly with their developers. Three trends: more cross-sector synergies, more open access, finer time detail for high-renewable futures.
items.why: Review of reviews — the best single map of the tool landscape.

items.title: National energy system optimization modelling for decarbonization pathways analysis: A systematic literature review
items.authors: Plazas-Niño, F.A., Ortiz-Pimiento, N.R., Montes-Páez, E.G.
items.finding: National optimisation models are mostly long-term, multi-sector, linear and assume perfect foresight; decarbonisation pathways are their main use.
items.why: Systematic (protocol-based) review focused on national planning models like TIMES and OSeMOSYS.

items.title: Next frontiers in energy system modelling: A review on challenges and the state of the art
items.authors: Fodstad, M., Crespo del Granado, P., Hellemo, L., et al.
items.finding: Four open frontiers: time and space, uncertainty, multi-energy systems, and consumer behaviour. Long-term models still handle uncertainty poorly, especially for emerging technologies.
items.why: Up-to-date research agenda for the field.

items.title: A systemic approach to analyze integrated energy system modeling tools: A review of national models
items.authors: Fattahi, A., Sijm, J., Faaij, A.
items.finding: Assesses 19 integrated national models for their ability to represent a low-carbon transition and identifies gaps (flexibility, sector coupling, social factors).
items.why: Useful checklist of what a national transition model should capture.

items.title: Are open source energy system optimization tools mature enough for serious use?
items.authors: Groissböck, M.
items.finding: Benchmarks open-source optimisation tools against commercial ones; several are capable, but gaps remain in some functionality.
items.why: Practical guide if you ever want to run models yourself.

items.title: Formalizing best practice for energy system optimization modelling
items.authors: DeCarolis, J., Daly, H., Dodds, P., et al.
items.finding: Sets out best practice: clear research questions, transparent assumptions, systematic uncertainty analysis, and framing results as insight rather than prediction.
items.why: The reference checklist for judging study quality.

items.title: Using modeling to generate alternatives (MGA) to expand our thinking on energy futures
items.authors: DeCarolis, J.F.
items.finding: Introduces MGA to energy models: search for very different systems that cost only slightly more than the optimum, since the single 'optimal' answer is fragile.
items.why: Foundational idea behind near-optimal analysis.

items.title: The near-optimal feasible space of a renewable power system model
items.authors: Neumann, F., Brown, T.
items.finding: Within a few percent of minimum cost, very different European power systems are possible, so policy has wide room to choose based on non-cost criteria.
items.why: Shows how flat the cost landscape is — key for reading 'least-cost' claims.

items.title: Does cost optimization approximate the real-world energy transition?
items.authors: Trutnevyte, E.
items.finding: Compared cost-optimal scenarios with the actual UK electricity transition and found large deviations; cost minimisation alone is a weak guide to real outcomes.
items.why: Rare empirical test of the core assumption behind optimisation models.

items.title: A review of approaches to uncertainty assessment in energy system optimization models
items.authors: Yue, X., Pye, S., DeCarolis, J., Li, F.G.N., Rogan, F., Ó Gallachóir, B.
items.finding: Compares Monte Carlo, stochastic programming, robust optimisation and MGA, and when each fits.
items.why: The go-to overview of uncertainty methods.

items.title: A modeler's guide to handle complexity in energy systems optimization
items.authors: Kotzur, L., Nolting, L., Hoffmann, M., et al.
items.finding: Reviews ways to keep models solvable (time-series aggregation, spatial clustering, decomposition) and how each affects accuracy.
items.why: Explains why model simplifications can change results.

items.title: Integrating short term variations of the power system into integrated energy system models: A methodological review
items.authors: Collins, S., Deane, J.P., Poncelet, K., et al.
items.finding: Long-term models with coarse time steps undervalue flexibility and overvalue variable renewables; reviews methods (soft-linking, representative days) to fix this.
items.why: Core reference on the time-resolution problem.

items.title: System integration of wind and solar power in integrated assessment models: A cross-model evaluation of new approaches
items.authors: Pietzcker, R.C., Ueckerdt, F., Carrara, S., et al.
items.finding: Evaluates how six IAMs represent variable renewables' integration challenges; newer approaches improved realism, with remaining gaps in storage and flexibility.
items.why: Shows how much IAM wind/solar results depend on integration modelling.

items.title: The importance of open data and software: Is energy research lagging behind?
items.authors: Pfenninger, S., DeCarolis, J., Hirth, L., Quoilin, S., Staffell, I.
items.finding: Argues that closed models and data undermine trust and reproducibility in energy policy research, and sets out how to open them.
items.why: Why open models (PyPSA, OSeMOSYS, Calliope) deserve more trust.

items.title: Optimising for the long game: methodological challenges in energy system optimisation pathways
items.authors: See preprint
items.finding: Systematic review of national-and-above pathway studies, focused on foresight assumptions, end-of-horizon effects and resolution choices that can bias model outcomes.
items.why: Recent; not yet peer-reviewed.

items.title: Plummeting costs of renewables — Are energy scenarios lagging?
items.authors: Xiao, M., Junne, T., Haas, J., Klein, M.
items.finding: Rapid declines in wind and solar costs have been structurally underestimated in nearly all scenario studies, so their future role tends to be underestimated too.
items.why: Quantifies a systematic bias in model inputs.

items.title: Empirically grounded technology forecasts and the energy transition
items.authors: Way, R., Ives, M.C., Mealy, P., Farmer, J.D.
items.finding: Uses cost-forecasting methods back-tested on 50+ technologies; a fast transition based on solar, wind, batteries and electrolysers likely saves trillions versus a fossil system, and a nuclear-led transition comes out far more expensive.
items.why: Empirically validated alternative to standard cost assumptions; its nuclear conclusion depends on historical nuclear cost trends.

items.title: Paving the way towards a sustainable future or lagging behind? An ex-post analysis of the International Energy Agency's World Energy Outlook
items.authors: Lopez, G., Pourjamal, Y., Breyer, C.
items.finding: Across WEO editions from 1993 to 2022, total demand growth was projected well, but fossil and nuclear growth were overestimated and key renewables severely underestimated.
items.why: Longest ex-post check of the most influential outlook.

items.title: Looking the wrong way: bias, renewable electricity, and energy modelling in the United States
items.authors: Gilbert, A.Q., Sovacool, B.K.
items.finding: Twelve years of US EIA Annual Energy Outlook projections consistently under-projected most renewable technologies, mainly due to model limitations and missing state policies.
items.why: Shows the same bias in the main US outlook.

items.title: The Role of Firm Low-Carbon Electricity Resources in Deep Decarbonization of Power Generation
items.authors: Sepulveda, N.A., Jenkins, J.D., de Sisternes, F.J., Lester, R.K.
items.finding: Across over 1,000 scenarios, every least-cost zero-carbon system includes at least one firm low-carbon resource; without them, costs rise steeply as emissions approach zero.
items.why: Introduced the 'firm / fuel-saving / fast-burst' taxonomy now used across the field.

items.title: The design space for long-duration energy storage in decarbonized power systems
items.authors: Sepulveda, N.A., Jenkins, J.D., Edington, A., Mallapragada, D.S., Lester, R.K.
items.finding: Maps the cost and efficiency combinations at which long-duration storage could displace firm generation; very low energy-capacity costs are needed.
items.why: Defines the targets storage must hit to compete with firm power such as nuclear.

items.title: Net-zero emissions energy systems
items.authors: Davis, S.J., Lewis, N.S., Shaner, M., et al.
items.finding: Identifies hard-to-decarbonise services (aviation, shipping, steel, cement, highly reliable electricity) and the technologies needed for them: firm power, storage, carbon-neutral fuels.
items.why: Framed the 'hard-to-abate' agenda.

items.title: System LCOE: What are the costs of variable renewables?
items.authors: Ueckerdt, F., Hirth, L., Luderer, G., Edenhofer, O.
items.finding: Defines 'system LCOE', adding integration costs to plant-level LCOE; integration costs can be substantial at high wind and solar shares.
items.why: Standard concept for comparing variable and firm technologies fairly.

items.title: The market value of variable renewables: The effect of solar wind power variability on their relative price
items.authors: Hirth, L.
items.finding: The market value of wind and solar falls as their share rises (the 'cannibalisation' effect), significantly at high penetration.
items.why: Foundational paper on value, not just cost, of variable renewables.

items.title: Synergies of sector coupling and transmission reinforcement in a cost-optimised, highly renewable European energy system
items.authors: Brown, T., Schlachtberger, D., Kies, A., Schramm, S., Greiner, M.
items.finding: Coupling power with heat and transport and reinforcing transmission both lower the cost of a highly renewable European system, and partially substitute for each other.
items.why: Landmark open-model (PyPSA) study on sector coupling.

items.title: Early decarbonisation of the European energy system pays off
items.authors: Victoria, M., Zhu, K., Brown, T., Andresen, G.B., Greiner, M.
items.finding: For the same carbon budget, an early, steady decarbonisation path costs about the same or less than a delayed one and avoids stranded assets.
items.why: Key study on transition timing, using an open model.

items.title: Stylized least-cost analysis of flexible nuclear power in deeply decarbonized electricity systems considering wind and solar resources worldwide
items.authors: Duan, L., Petroski, R., Wood, L., Caldeira, K.
items.finding: Across many countries' wind and solar resources, nuclear's role in least-cost deep-decarbonised systems depends mostly on its cost relative to wind, solar and storage; added flexibility helps modestly.
items.why: Global, resource-aware look at when nuclear earns a place.

items.title: Nexus-e: A platform of interfaced high-resolution models for energy-economic assessments of future electricity systems
items.authors: Gjorgiev, B., Garrison, J.B., Han, X., et al.
items.finding: ETH Zurich's linked-model platform for the Swiss electricity system, connecting macro-economy, investment, operation and grid models.
items.why: Key Swiss modelling framework used to study nuclear phase-out and net-zero options.
